lead: The ideal-gas law, PV = nRT, is the simplest equation of state. It treats molecules as points with no attractions, so pressure, volume and temperature are tied by one equation. That makes every path calculable: heat, work and internal-energy change follow from the path and the gas. Engineers use it for a first estimate of compressor duty, pipeline pressure drop, or the air in a tyre. It is also the reference state against which real gases are measured. This chapter fixes the sign convention, lists the five common paths, and works one numerical example.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.1 for P–V diagrams, and Unit 1 for the first law, enthalpy and heat capacities.

sections.h3: The ideal-gas law and its energy

blocks.text: The ideal-gas law is PV = nRT. P is absolute pressure, V is volume, n is amount in moles, R is the gas constant, and T is absolute temperature in kelvin. Use R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ = 0.08314 L bar mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. The second value matches litres and bar, so use it when V is in L and P in bar. Never put T in °C; 25 °C is 298.15 K, not 25.

For an ideal gas, molecules have no volume and no forces except elastic collisions. That model makes internal energy U a function of T only. Enthalpy H = U + PV is also a function of T only, because PV = nRT. So an isothermal change has ΔU = 0 and ΔH = 0, even when P and V change. This is the key fact behind all paths below.
PV = nRT; C<sub>p</sub> − C<sub>v</sub> = R; γ = C<sub>p</sub>/C<sub>v</sub>
blocks.where: P is absolute pressure; V is volume; n is moles; R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ = 0.08314 L bar mol⁻¹ K⁻¹; T is absolute temperature in K; C<sub>p</sub> and C<sub>v</sub> are molar heat capacities at constant pressure and volume; γ is the heat-capacity ratio.

blocks.text: Heat capacities follow from that. C<sub>v</sub> = (∂U/∂T)<sub>V</sub> and C<sub>p</sub> = (∂H/∂T)<sub>P</sub>. For an ideal gas C<sub>p</sub> − C<sub>v</sub> = R and γ = C<sub>p</sub>/C<sub>v</sub>. C<sub>v</sub> is the heat needed to raise 1 mol by 1 K at constant volume; C<sub>p</sub> is the same at constant pressure. For a diatomic gas near room temperature, C<sub>v</sub> ≈ (5/2)R and C<sub>p</sub> ≈ (7/2)R, so γ ≈ 1.4. Monatomic gases have γ ≈ 1.67.

sections.h3: Five paths and one sign convention

blocks.text: Use W as work done by the gas on the surroundings. Then the first law for a closed system is ΔU = Q − W. Q is heat added to the gas; W is positive for expansion and negative for compression. State this convention before any calculation.

blocks.where: ΔU is change in internal energy; Q is heat added to the gas; W is work done by the gas on the surroundings.

blocks.text: Each path fixes one quantity. Integrate W = ∫P dV along the path. The table gives closed-system results for an ideal gas with constant C<sub>v</sub> and C<sub>p</sub>; ΔT = T<sub>2</sub> − T<sub>1</sub>. The work formulas are for reversible paths; for irreversible paths use the actual external pressure.

An isochoric path has no volume change, so W = 0; all heat goes into U. An isobaric path expands against constant pressure, so W = PΔV and Q = ΔH. An isothermal path keeps U and H fixed; heat and work cancel. An adiabatic path has Q = 0; work comes from U, so expansion cools the gas. Also PV<sup>γ</sup> = constant, TV<sup>γ−1</sup> = constant and TP<sup>(1−γ)/γ</sup> = constant. A polytropic path PV<sup>k</sup> = constant uses k, the polytropic exponent; it covers the range between isothermal (k = 1) and adiabatic (k = γ); for k = 1 use the isothermal formula.
Some syllabi call these non-flow processes. The flow version for nozzles and compressors is in Unit 1; do not mix the two.

sections.h3: Mixtures and the limit of the model

blocks.text: For a mixture of ideal gases, each component i obeys PiV = niRT, where Pi is its partial pressure and ni its moles. The total pressure is P = ΣPi = nRT/V, with n = Σni. This is Dalton's law in ideal-gas form. The mixture's U and H depend on T only, and its Cv and Cp are mole-fraction averages of the pure-component values. Treat this as a limiting case; real mixtures need fugacity.

The ideal-gas law is accurate at low pressure and high temperature, when molecules are far apart. At high pressure or near condensation, use the compressibility factor or a cubic equation of state. The simple paths in this chapter still give the limiting behaviour and a first estimate for compressor and pipeline calculations.

figure.caption: Three paths from 24.94 L to 12.47 L for 1 mol at 300 K: the isothermal ends at 2.00 bar, the adiabatic at 2.64 bar, and the isobaric stays at 1.00 bar.

spec.aria: Pressure–volume plot for 1 mol of ideal gas at 300 K from 24.94 L: three paths to 12.47 L; the isothermal ends at 2.00 bar, the adiabatic at 2.64 bar and the isobaric stays at 1.00 bar.

examples.question: One mole of an ideal gas is at 300 K and 1.00 bar. Its volume is 24.94 L. It is taken to 12.47 L by three separate paths: (a) isothermal, (b) adiabatic with γ = 1.4, (c) isobaric. Find the final pressure for each path. Use R = 0.08314 L bar mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
steps: Find the initial volume from PV = nRT: V<sub>1</sub> = nRT<sub>1</sub>/P<sub>1</sub> = (1 mol)(0.08314 L bar mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)(300 K)/(1.00 bar) = 24.94 L. This matches the given value.
(a) Isothermal: T is constant, so P<sub>1</sub>V<sub>1</sub> = P<sub>2</sub>V<sub>2</sub>. P<sub>2</sub> = P<sub>1</sub>V<sub>1</sub>/V<sub>2</sub> = (1.00 bar)(24.94 L)/(12.47 L) = 2.00 bar.

(b) Adiabatic: PV<sup>γ</sup> = constant, so P<sub>2</sub> = P<sub>1</sub>(V<sub>1</sub>/V<sub>2</sub>)<sup>γ</sup>. The volume ratio is 24.94/12.47 = 2.000. P<sub>2</sub> = (1.00 bar)(2.000)<sup>1.4</sup> = 2.64 bar.
(c) Isobaric: P is fixed. P<sub>2</sub> = P<sub>1</sub> = 1.00 bar.

Check the volume ratio and units: L cancels in the ratio; pressure stays in bar. The adiabatic final pressure is higher than the isothermal one because compression work raises the gas temperature above 300 K (T₂ ≈ 396 K here). At the same smaller volume, a higher T gives a higher P; in the isothermal path T stays at 300 K.
examples.check:
n = 1.0
R = 0.08314
T1 = 300.0
P1 = 1.0
V2 = 12.47
gamma = 1.4
V1 = n * R * T1 / P1
P_iso = P1 * V1 / V2
P_ad = P1 * (V1 / V2) ** gamma
P_isob = P1
print(round(P_iso, 2))
print(round(P_ad, 2))
print(round(P_isob, 2))

traps: PV<sup>γ</sup> = constant is for adiabatic, not isothermal. Isothermal is PV = constant; using γ there gives a wrong final pressure.
Put T in kelvin. 27 °C is 300 K; using 27 in PV = nRT is a large error.
State the W sign convention. Many engineering texts take W by gas positive (ΔU = Q − W); many chemistry texts take W on gas positive (ΔU = Q + W). Mixing them flips Q.
For a rigid tank use C<sub>v</sub>, not C<sub>p</sub>. Q = nC<sub>v</sub>ΔT for isochoric; Q = nC<sub>p</sub>ΔT for isobaric.
Adiabatic does not mean isothermal. Q = 0, but T changes and W = nC<sub>v</sub>(T<sub>1</sub> − T<sub>2</sub>) is not zero.

quiz.q: State the ideal-gas law and give R in both J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and L bar mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
quiz.a: PV = nRT; R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ = 0.08314 L bar mol⁻¹ K⁻¹; T must be in K.

quiz.q: Why is ΔU zero for an isothermal change of an ideal gas, even when V changes?
quiz.a: Ideal-gas U depends only on T. If T is constant, U is constant, so ΔU = 0. Work is balanced by heat.

quiz.q: 2 mol of ideal gas expands isothermally and reversibly at 300 K from 10 L to 20 L. Find W done by the gas. Use R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
1 mol of ideal gas with γ = 1.4 is compressed adiabatically and reversibly from 1.00 bar and 300 K to 5.00 bar. Find T₂.
At the same (P, V) point, which curve is steeper on a P–V diagram: isothermal or adiabatic? Give the slope reason.
quiz.a: Adiabatic is steeper. Slope is −P/V for isothermal and −γP/V for adiabatic; γ > 1, so the adiabatic slope magnitude is larger.

quiz.q: In the W-on-gas convention ΔU = Q + W, expansion work is W = −PΔV. If a student wrongly writes W = +PΔV, is the Q obtained too high or too low, and by how much? Use the correct value as reference.
quiz.a: The Q obtained is too low by 2PΔV. Correct: Q = ΔU + PΔV. With W = +PΔV the equation gives Q = ΔU − PΔV, which is 2PΔV smaller.

beyond: Not for the exam. Process simulators use the ideal-gas law as the first pass, then switch to cubic equations of state or compressibility correlations near the dew point. The same path formulas appear in compressor sizing, but with efficiency and flow terms added. Search for ideal-gas polytropic compression and compressibility-factor generalized correlation to go further.
